newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND- US trade gap relief after rocky '97 start.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND- US trade gap relief after rocky '97 start.

text.p: Persistent sluggishness in the economies of Europe and Japan and steady, albeit modest, U.S. growth should combine to cast a dark shadow over a ballooning U.S. trade gap in the early stages of 1997, experts predicted.
But the prospects for dollar weakness and the promise of an Asian economic recovery in the latter half of the year do offer a glimmer of hope for the nagging imbalance in the longer term.
"Trade deficits tend to react with a bit of a lag to changes in growth rates so I think it probably gets worse before it gets better," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at Barclays Bank in New York.

"Certainly in the second half of the year some stronger growth numbers from the overseas markets could lead to some turnaround in the trade picture but you're still talking of monthly average deficits in the first part of the year above $10 or $11 billion," Iggo added.
The U.S. trade deficit has risen steadily in recent years, despite government efforts to make the reduction of trade imbalances a key objective of foreign policy.

Earlier this week, the U.S. Commerce Department reported that sagging exports and a liquidation of U.S. stock holdings on the part of foreign investors had helped drive the U.S. current account deficit to a record $47.96 billion in the third quarter.
Officials have blamed the deteriorating trade numbers on the strength of import demand, while lauding the resiliency of exports in the face of lackluster foreign economic performance.

And although exports have generally been firm of late, a $3.2 billion dip in the recent third quarter figures raises concerns that continued sluggishness overseas and the rising value of the dollar could begin cutting into export gains.

On Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, whose strong dollar mantra has helped push the greenback off post-World War II lows reached in early 1995, reiterated his opposition to using dollar depreciation to boost U.S. competitiveness.
Rubin blamed the massive deficit on subpar overseas growth, a phenomenon which is unlikely to reverse itself any time soon.

"If we just look at generic overseas growth as continuing to underperform the U.S. at least through the first half of the year, that will be putting more pressure on the U.S. trade deficit, no matter what the currency does," said Richard Koss, international economist at MFR Inc.
Koss predicts a year-over-year widening of roughly $20 billion in the trade deficit.

He expects a steady to slightly firmer dollar in the early part of the year, then a gradual slide in the greenback's value as growth picks up overseas. He noted a risk of an earlier drop in the dollar if the trade burden gets too unwieldy.
Experts agree that another potential risk to the dollar lies in the heady holdings of U.S. securities in countries such as China.
Recently, as the U.S. bilateral trade deficit with Japan has narrowed, the imbalance with China has grown more acute. China's bilateral surplus has fed heavy purchases of U.S. government debt.
"China, because of its trade surplus with the U.S., is building up massive holdings of dollars which it has been using to buy Treasury securities with this year," said Barclay's Iggo.
"The mere threat of selling those Treasuries and moving the funds into another currency would have a very negative impact on the dollar and on Treasuries," he added.
Signs of weaker U.S. growth do offer some promise of relief for the trade imbalance, economists said.
Recent retail sales and payrolls data suggest the U.S. economy is indeed cooling off after a torrid third quarter, and that could lead to a slowing in domestic demand for foreign goods.
"I'm expecting U.S. growth to decelerate and that means our appetite for imports should be more moderate," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
Sohn believes the Japanese economy is showing signs of reawakening, but predicted continued weakness in Europe as it prepares for Economic and Monetary Union.
Robert Hormats, vice chairman at Goldman Sachs International agreed, and said foreign growth could be the wild card for U.S. markets in the year ahead.

"There is a risk that without a pickup in growth abroad, we could suffer from a very substantial widening of the trade deficit, which in turn would lead to greater skepticism about the dollar," he said. "Trade is certainly going to play a more important part in the market this year than last."
